script.opening: (Light, apologetic, playing it down.) "This is probably nothing — I've been getting double vision on and off for a few weeks, usually when I'm tired or after a lot of screen time. It comes and goes. Oh, and a couple of weeks ago I had some blurry, achy vision in my left eye for a few days. I just figured I needed more sleep. Can you reassure me it's just eye strain?"

facts.text: About 4 weeks, several times a day, lasting minutes to an hour. If asked to cover each eye during an episode: "Actually, yes, whichever eye I cover, it goes. I hadn't really thought about that." "Mostly side by side, I think. Sometimes a bit tilted."

"Definitely worse in the evenings. I'm not sure about the eyelids. Nobody's said anything." If asked: her arms ache doing her hair at the end of the day. No trouble swallowing, chewing or speaking, no breathlessness — "No, nothing like that."
"Yes, it ached when I looked around, and everything looked a bit washed out. It's mostly better now." Lasted about 5 days, two weeks ago. Colours (red) still look a bit faded in that eye.
"Not that I can think of." If asked specifically: a year ago, tingling in both legs for two weeks that went away. No weakness, bladder problems or balance problems now.
"No headaches really. No." No sudden severe headache, no droopy eyelid with a big pupil, no vomiting.
No medicines, no allergies. Combined pill. Thyroid: never checked. Non-smoker. Graphic designer, long hours at screens. Drives to work.
Aunt has "thyroid problems". No MS in the family she knows of.

"(pause) I suppose I've been avoiding thinking about it. If it's just tiredness I don't have to worry. If it's not… I don't want to hear it's something like MS." Her friend's mum has MS and uses a wheelchair.

Minimising and hoping for reassurance. Honest when asked. When MS is mentioned: "So it could be MS?" — relieved by balanced information. Surprised by the urgency: "Today? Is that really necessary?" — then agrees: "I can get there this afternoon." Hadn't thought about driving.

ice.ideas: "It's tiredness and too much screen time."
ice.concerns: HIDDEN AGENDA — she has quietly wondered about MS (a friend's mother has it) and has been avoiding the thought.

cues: "Blurry, achy vision in my left eye." — mentioned as an aside; possible optic neuritis.
"I don't want to hear it's something like MS." — the fear, if explored.

checkpoints.text: Distinguishes MONOCULAR (ocular/refractive, less sinister) from BINOCULAR diplopia (neurological/neuromuscular, concerning) by asking whether covering one eye resolves it

Considers MULTIPLE SCLEROSIS in a young woman — recognises the recent painful monocular visual disturbance as likely OPTIC NEURITIS and the principle of episodes separated in time/space — warranting urgent neurology/ophthalmology and MRI
Considers MYASTHENIA GRAVIS — screens FATIGABLE diplopia/ptosis (worse end of day/with effort), bulbar (swallow/speech) and limb fatigue — and recognises the risk of bulbar/respiratory compromise

Knows the cranial-nerve RED FLAGS — painful III palsy with a FIXED DILATED PUPIL (posterior communicating aneurysm — emergency), VI palsy as a false-localising sign of RAISED ICP — and screens accordingly (headache, papilloedema, vomiting)

Arranges an in-person EXAMINATION today (acuity, pupils/RAPD, eye movements, ptosis and fatigability, fundi, neuro screen — not possible on video) and sets URGENCY by findings — emergency for pupil-involving III palsy/thunderclap headache/raised ICP/bulbar or breathing symptoms; same-day on-call ophthalmology or neurology discussion for new persistent binocular diplopia; urgent neurology ± ophthalmology/MRI otherwise (NICE NG220; ABN; NICE NG12 direct-access MRI route)
Reads the minimisation/wish for reassurance, takes recurrent neurological symptoms seriously, and does NOT collude with "it’s just eye strain/tiredness"
Communicates the need for urgent assessment honestly without catastrophising, explains the reasoning, and checks understanding

Safety-nets and refers with appropriate urgency: emergency advice for red flags (sudden severe headache, painful eye with dilated pupil, swallowing/breathing difficulty), urgent neurology/ophthalmology referral and MRI as indicated, the DVLA duty (no driving with diplopia; she must tell the DVLA) advised and documented, and follow-up — not reassurance as tiredness

worked.txt: "I’m glad you came, and I’d love to reassure you — but double vision that keeps happening, plus that painful blurry episode in one eye, are things I need to take seriously rather than put down to screens. Let me ask some specific questions."

"When you get the double vision, does it disappear if you cover one eye — either eye? … It only goes when you cover one. That tells me it’s the kind that comes from the eyes not aligning, which points to a nerve or muscle cause rather than simple eye strain."

"That eye that was painful and blurry for a few days — was it sore to move? Any numbness, weakness or balance problems before? And the double vision — is it worse at the end of the day or when you’re tired? Any trouble swallowing or slurring when tired?"

"I can’t check your eye movements, pupils, eyelids or the back of your eyes properly over video, so I want you seen in person today. Any new severe headache, or a painful eye with a big pupil? Those would be urgent in a different way — I’m checking for them."

"I’m not going to label this tiredness. The painful eye episode could have been inflammation of the eye nerve, and with the double vision I want you examined today, and a brain scan and a neurologist’s opinion urgently. While you have double vision you mustn’t drive, and the law says you need to tell the DVLA. It might be nothing serious, but these are things we don’t sit on."

"Before you’re seen: if you get a sudden severe headache, a painful eye with a dilated pupil, weakness, or any trouble swallowing or breathing, that’s an emergency — 999. I’ll arrange the referral and scan now and we’ll follow it through together."

f.learning: Diplopia in a young adult is approached structurally. First split MONOCULAR (persists with one eye open, resolves only when that eye is covered — usually an ocular/refractive/lens problem, less sinister) from BINOCULAR diplopia (present with both eyes open, resolves when EITHER eye is covered — implying ocular misalignment from a neurological or neuromuscular cause), the latter being the concerning type that demands a neuro work-up. In a young woman, consider MULTIPLE SCLEROSIS — her recent painful, blurred monocular visual episode is a classic description of OPTIC NEURITIS (pain on eye movement, reduced acuity/colour vision, often resolving), and MS produces episodes separated in time and space (e.g. internuclear ophthalmoplegia) — warranting urgent neurology/ophthalmology and MRI, not "tiredness". Consider MYASTHENIA GRAVIS, which causes FATIGABLE diplopia and ptosis worse with effort and toward the end of the day, with possible bulbar (swallow/speech) and limb fatigue and a risk of bulbar/respiratory compromise (myasthenic crisis). Know the cranial-nerve RED FLAGS: a painful THIRD nerve palsy with a FIXED DILATED PUPIL is a posterior communicating artery ANEURYSM until proven otherwise — a neurosurgical emergency — and a SIXTH nerve palsy can be a false-localising sign of RAISED INTRACRANIAL PRESSURE (screen headache, papilloedema, vomiting). Examine acuity, pupils (RAPD), eye movements, ptosis and fatigability, and fundi IN PERSON (on video, arrange a same-day face-to-face examination), and set urgency by findings — emergency for a pupil-involving III palsy, thunderclap headache (NICE NG228), raised ICP with papilloedema or bulbar/breathing symptoms; same-day on-call ophthalmology or neurology discussion for new persistent binocular diplopia or current visual loss; urgent neurology ± ophthalmology and MRI for suspected MS/optic neuritis (NICE NG220) or ocular myasthenia (ABN guidelines). Advise that a driver with diplopia must stop driving and tell the DVLA. The hidden agenda is the wish to be reassured it is just tiredness/screens while minimising recurrent neurological symptoms; take them seriously, work the serious differential and red flags, and refer with appropriate urgency honestly but without catastrophising — never colluding with "it’s just eye strain". NICE NG12 (Suspected cancer: recognition and referral, last updated April 2026) offers a route rather than a cancer label here: consider an urgent direct-access MRI brain (within 2 weeks) for progressive, sub-acute loss of central neurological function.

knowledge.summary: Recurrent binocular double vision in a young woman, with a recent painful blurred-vision episode in one eye, is neurological until proved otherwise. Split monocular from binocular, screen for optic neuritis, fatigable weakness and red flags, get her examined in person today, and refer with the right urgency.

points.t: Ask whether the double image goes when either eye is covered. Monocular diplopia (persists through one eye alone) is usually ocular: refractive error, cataract, corneal or lens problems. Binocular diplopia (goes when either eye is covered) means the eyes are misaligned, from a cranial nerve, neuromuscular junction, muscle or orbital cause, and needs a neurological assessment.

A few days of blurred vision in one eye with pain, especially on eye movement, and duller colours is the classic story of optic neuritis. NICE NG220 [1]: if isolated optic neuritis is confirmed by an ophthalmologist, refer to a consultant neurologist; a consultant neurologist makes the diagnosis of MS using history, examination, MRI and the revised McDonald criteria (lesions disseminated in time and space). Diplopia from an internuclear ophthalmoplegia would be a second, separate site.

Fatigable weakness: double vision or drooping lids that worsen as the day goes on or with sustained gaze and improve with rest. Ask about chewing or swallowing fatigue, slurred or nasal speech, neck and limb weakness, and breathlessness. ABN guidelines [3]: diagnosis and treatment are specialist-led (AChR antibodies are positive in about half of purely ocular cases). Bulbar or breathing symptoms risk a myasthenic crisis and need emergency assessment.

A third nerve palsy with a dilated pupil, especially with headache or eye pain, is a posterior communicating artery aneurysm until proved otherwise: 999 or emergency department now. A sixth nerve palsy can be a false-localising sign of raised intracranial pressure: ask about headache worse lying down or on straining, vomiting and transient visual obscurations. Thunderclap headache peaking within minutes is a subarachnoid haemorrhage question (NICE NG228 [5]).

Acuity, colour vision, pupils including a relative afferent pupillary defect, eye movements in all directions with a cover test, ptosis and fatigability on sustained upgaze, fundi for disc swelling, and a brief neurological screen. None of this can be done reliably on video, so arrange an in-person examination today.

Emergency (999 or ED): pupil-involving third nerve palsy, thunderclap headache, bulbar or breathing symptoms, or signs of raised pressure with papilloedema. Same day: new persistent binocular diplopia or current visual loss, discussed with on-call ophthalmology or neurology. Urgent: suspected MS or ocular myasthenia once emergencies are excluded. NICE NG12 [2]: consider an urgent direct-access MRI brain (within 2 weeks) for progressive, sub-acute loss of central neurological function.

DVLA [4]: a driver with diplopia must stop driving and tell the DVLA. Driving may restart only once the DVLA accepts that the diplopia is controlled, for example with a patch or prisms. The patient holds the legal duty; the doctor advises and records the advice.

model.text: Hello Erin, I’m Dr Patel. Can you hear and see me clearly? … Good. Tell me what’s been happening, from the beginning.
model.why: Checks the video link, then an open question

model.text: This is probably nothing. I’ve been getting double vision on and off for a few weeks, usually when I’m tired or after a lot of screen time. And a couple of weeks ago my left eye went blurry and achy for a few days. I just figured I needed more sleep. Can you tell me it’s eye strain?
I can hear you’d really like it to be eye strain, and I’d like that too. I’ll be honest with you as we go. Can I ask some specific questions first, so any reassurance I give is real?
model.why: Names her wish without colluding and explains why the questions matter

model.text: Okay. Go on.
When the double vision comes, if you cover one eye, does it go away? And does it go if you cover the other eye instead?
model.why: The first split: monocular versus binocular

model.text: Actually, yes, whichever eye I cover, it goes. I hadn’t really thought about that.

That’s really useful. It means the two eyes aren’t lining up, which comes from the nerves or muscles that move the eyes rather than tired eyes. Are the two pictures side by side, or one above the other?
model.why: Interprets binocular diplopia and begins to localise

model.text: Mostly side by side, I think. Sometimes a bit tilted.
Is it worse as the day goes on, or if you keep looking at something for a while, and better after a rest? Have your eyelids ever drooped?
Definitely worse in the evenings. I’m not sure about the eyelids. Nobody’s said anything.
Any tiredness when chewing or swallowing, your voice going slurred or nasal, trouble lifting your arms or holding your head up, or feeling short of breath?
model.why: Screens bulbar, limb and respiratory involvement

model.text: No, nothing like that.
Now that left eye. When it went blurry, did it hurt to move the eye? Were colours duller, especially reds?
Yes, it ached when I looked around, and everything looked a bit washed out. It’s mostly better now.
Have you ever had any numbness, tingling, weakness, problems with balance or with your bladder, lasting days, at any time before?
model.why: Looks for earlier episodes separated in time and place

model.text: Not that I can think of.

A few quick safety checks. Any sudden severe headache, or headache worse lying down or when you strain, being sick, or your vision greying out for a few seconds? Any pain around one eye with the lid drooping?
model.why: Screens aneurysm, SAH and raised intracranial pressure red flags

model.text: No headaches really. No.
You said at the start it’s probably nothing. Has any part of you wondered whether it might be something more?
(pause) I suppose I’ve been avoiding thinking about it. If it’s just tiredness I don’t have to worry. If it’s not… I don’t want to hear it’s something like MS.

Thank you for telling me that. It makes complete sense to want it to be the simple answer. I won’t guess at a diagnosis today, but I also won’t tell you it’s tiredness when I don’t think that’s been shown. Is that fair?
model.why: Validates the fear and is honest without catastrophising

model.text: Yes. I’d rather know.

Here’s my thinking. Double vision that goes when either eye is covered points to the eye-moving nerves or muscles. The painful blurry episode sounds like inflammation of the nerve at the back of the eye, called optic neuritis. There are a few possible causes. One is MS. Another is a condition where muscles tire easily, called myasthenia, which fits it being worse in the evenings. None of these are confirmed, and the specialists need to examine you and do tests.
model.why: Shares a reasoned differential in plain language

model.text: So it could be MS?

It’s one of the things they’ll want to look for, and I’d rather you heard that from me honestly. MS is diagnosed by a neurologist, with a scan and an examination, and only if it meets strict criteria. Not everyone who has an episode like this goes on to have MS, and if it is MS, treatment is much better than it used to be.
model.why: Answers directly, gives proportion without false reassurance

model.text: Okay. That helps a bit.

What I can’t do over video is look properly at your eyes: your pupils, the eye movements, your eyelids when you look up for a while, and the back of your eyes. So I’d like you to come in today so a doctor can examine you face to face.
model.why: Recognises video limits; arranges same-day in-person examination

model.text: Today? Is that really necessary?

I think so. Depending on what we find, I’ll speak to the eye team or the neurologists today, and they’ll decide how quickly to see you and when to do a brain scan. I’ll also refer you to the neurologists about the eye episode and the double vision, marked urgent.
model.why: Sets urgency by findings; same-day specialist advice; urgent neurology

model.text: Okay. I can get there this afternoon.
One more practical thing. If you drive, please don’t while you’re getting double vision. The law says you must stop and tell the DVLA. When it’s controlled, driving can usually be looked at again.
model.why: Gives the DVLA advice without inventing whether she drives

model.text: Right. I hadn’t thought about that.

Before you come in, call 999 or go to A&E if you get a sudden severe headache, a painful eye with a drooping lid or one pupil much bigger, any trouble swallowing, slurred speech or breathing, or new weakness. Those would need attention straight away.
model.why: Specific emergency safety-net in plain words

model.text: Okay. Headache, pupil, swallowing, breathing, weakness.
Exactly that. So, can you tell me back what the plan is, so I know I’ve explained it properly?
Come in this afternoon to be examined, you’ll talk to the specialists, there’s an urgent referral, no driving with double vision, and 999 for those warning signs.
Perfect. I’ll ring you after the specialists have given their view so you’re not left waiting in the dark. Is there anything you’d like to ask?
model.why: Defined follow-up and ownership of the result

model.text: No. Thank you for being straight with me.

social.t: Young adults with new neurological symptoms often explain them away (screens, stress, tiredness) because the alternative feels frightening. Naming the fear gently makes it possible to plan.
Double vision affects screen work, reading and travel. Temporary occlusion (a patch or frosted lens) may be advised by the specialist team; a fit note can cover time off work if needed.

legal.t: DVLA Assessing fitness to drive: a driver with diplopia must stop driving and notify the DVLA. Driving may resume only when the DVLA accepts the diplopia is controlled (for example patch or prisms). A later diagnosis such as MS or myasthenia has its own notification rules. The doctor advises and documents; the duty to notify is the patient’s.

professional.t: GMC remote consultations guidance: if a remote consultation cannot provide a safe assessment, arrange a face-to-face one. Eye movements, pupils and fundi need examination in person.
Share the possible causes honestly when asked, including MS, while being clear that nothing is confirmed. Document the discussion, the red-flag screen, the urgency set and the safety-net.

community.t: The MS Society and the Myaware charity provide information once a specialist diagnosis is made; do not signpost to condition-specific groups before diagnosis unless she asks.

redFlags: Painful third nerve palsy or a dilated pupil with ptosis: aneurysm until proved otherwise (999/ED)
Thunderclap headache, headache worse lying down or on straining, vomiting, transient visual obscurations (SAH or raised intracranial pressure)
Swallowing, speech or breathing difficulty with fatigable weakness (myasthenic crisis risk)
Persisting visual loss in one eye
psychosocial: Screen-based work and how the symptoms affect it
Her anxiety and tendency to explain symptoms away
ice: Idea: tiredness or eye strain from screens
Concern: unspoken fear of something serious such as MS
Expectation: to be reassured it is eye strain

playbook.diagnosis: “Double vision that disappears when either eye is covered means the eyes aren’t lining up, so it comes from the nerves or muscles that move them. With the painful blurry episode in your left eye, which sounds like inflammation of the eye nerve, this needs a specialist neurological assessment rather than being put down to tiredness.”
playbook.diagnosisLay: “Your two eyes are like a pair of cameras that have to point at exactly the same spot. When the double picture vanishes whichever eye you cover, it tells me the cameras are slightly out of line, and that’s about the wiring and the muscles, not tired eyes.”

management.reflectIce: “You said you’d been avoiding thinking about it because you were scared it might be MS. I’m not going to guess today, but I’m also not going to call it tiredness when I don’t think that’s been shown.”
management.psychosocial: Acknowledge the fear, give proportion (several possible causes; one episode does not always mean MS), and keep her involved in every step so she is not left waiting alone.
sharedPlan: Face-to-face examination today (acuity, colour, pupils/RAPD, eye movements, fatigable ptosis, fundi, neuro screen)
Same-day discussion with on-call ophthalmology or neurology based on findings
Urgent neurology referral; imaging and antibody tests per specialist advice
No driving while diplopic; notify the DVLA if she drives
safetyNet: 999/ED for sudden severe headache, painful eye with drooping lid or enlarged pupil, swallowing, speech or breathing difficulty, or new weakness
Call-back after the specialist view; review promptly if symptoms change

pitfalls.intro: This station is failed by candidates who accept the patient’s own explanation. Binocular double vision plus a probable optic neuritis in a 29-year-old needs a proper neurological assessment, and the video format adds the trap of pretending to examine.

items.fail: Never asking whether the double vision goes when one eye is covered.
items.why: “Data gathering not sufficiently focused.” The monocular versus binocular split is the single most discriminating question in diplopia.
items.fix: Ask it in the first two minutes: “If you cover one eye, does it go? And the other eye?”

items.fail: Missing the painful blurred-vision episode because it was mentioned in passing.
items.why: Optic neuritis is the key clue to a demyelinating cause; missing it leads to a routine plan.
items.fix: Return to it: “Tell me more about the left eye. Did it hurt to move it? Were colours duller?”

items.fail: “Examining” pupils and eye movements over video and declaring them normal.
items.why: Unsafe and not credible. Examiners expect you to recognise the limits of a remote consultation.
items.fix: “I can’t check this properly on video. I’d like you examined in person today.”

items.fail: Reassuring her that it is eye strain because that is what she asked for.
items.why: “Colludes with the patient” and misses the hidden fear driving the minimisation.
items.fix: “I can hear you’d like it to be eye strain. I’ll be honest with you as we go.” Then ask whether she has wondered if it is more.

items.fail: Announcing “this could be MS” early, then listing its complications.
items.why: Catastrophising damages trust and is not supported until a neurologist has assessed her.
items.fix: Offer the differential honestly and proportionately: several possible causes, nothing confirmed, specialists will decide.

items.fail: Referring “urgently” with no timescale, no red-flag advice and no mention of driving.
items.why: Non-specific safety-netting and an omitted DVLA duty are standard failing feedback.
items.fix: Same-day examination, named 999 symptoms, conditional DVLA advice, and a promised call-back.

Cover-one-eye question, direction of images, fatigability and bulbar symptoms, optic neuritis features, previous neurological episodes, red-flag headache and pupil questions.
Ask gently whether she has wondered if it is more than tiredness. The fear of MS surfaces.

Binocular means nerves or muscles, not eye strain. Name optic neuritis and the possible causes honestly. Same-day face-to-face examination, same-day specialist advice, urgent neurology. DVLA advice if she drives.
999 triggers in plain words, teach-back, and a promised call-back after the specialist view.

wordPics.pass: Establishes binocular diplopia, recognises probable optic neuritis and fatigable features, screens the red flags, arranges an in-person examination and an urgent specialist referral, and safety-nets for emergencies.
wordPics.exc: All of the above, plus: draws out the unspoken fear of MS and answers it honestly and proportionately; explains why video cannot replace the examination; sets urgency by findings with same-day specialist advice; gives DVLA advice without assuming she drives; teach-back and a promised call-back.

avoid.dont: “It’s probably just eye strain from your screens. Try the 20-20-20 rule.”
avoid.instead: “Double vision that goes when either eye is covered comes from the nerves or muscles, not tired eyes, so I need to look into it properly.”
avoid.why: Colluding with her minimisation is the failing move in this station.

avoid.instead: “There are several possible causes and one the specialists will look for is MS. Not everyone with one episode like this develops it.”
avoid.why: Naming a frightening diagnosis as likely, before assessment, is catastrophising.

avoid.dont: “Follow my finger with your eyes… your pupils look fine on camera.”
avoid.instead: “I can’t check your eyes properly on video, so I’d like you examined in person today.”
avoid.why: Pupils, fundi and fatigability cannot be judged reliably over video; pretending otherwise is unsafe.

SCA_MODELS.why: Names her wish without colluding and explains why the questions matter

SCA_MODELS.text: Okay. Go on.
When the double vision comes, if you cover one eye, does it go away? And does it go if you cover the other eye instead?
SCA_MODELS.why: The first split: monocular versus binocular

SCA_MODELS.text: Actually, yes, whichever eye I cover, it goes. I hadn’t really thought about that.

That’s really useful. It means the two eyes aren’t lining up, which comes from the nerves or muscles that move the eyes rather than tired eyes. Are the two pictures side by side, or one above the other?
SCA_MODELS.why: Interprets binocular diplopia and begins to localise

SCA_MODELS.text: Mostly side by side, I think. Sometimes a bit tilted.
Is it worse as the day goes on, or if you keep looking at something for a while, and better after a rest? Have your eyelids ever drooped?
Definitely worse in the evenings. I’m not sure about the eyelids. Nobody’s said anything.
Any tiredness when chewing or swallowing, your voice going slurred or nasal, trouble lifting your arms or holding your head up, or feeling short of breath?
SCA_MODELS.why: Screens bulbar, limb and respiratory involvement

SCA_MODELS.text: No, nothing like that.
Now that left eye. When it went blurry, did it hurt to move the eye? Were colours duller, especially reds?
Yes, it ached when I looked around, and everything looked a bit washed out. It’s mostly better now.
Have you ever had any numbness, tingling, weakness, problems with balance or with your bladder, lasting days, at any time before?
SCA_MODELS.why: Looks for earlier episodes separated in time and place

SCA_MODELS.text: Not that I can think of.

A few quick safety checks. Any sudden severe headache, or headache worse lying down or when you strain, being sick, or your vision greying out for a few seconds? Any pain around one eye with the lid drooping?
SCA_MODELS.why: Screens aneurysm, SAH and raised intracranial pressure red flags

SCA_MODELS.text: No headaches really. No.
You said at the start it’s probably nothing. Has any part of you wondered whether it might be something more?
(pause) I suppose I’ve been avoiding thinking about it. If it’s just tiredness I don’t have to worry. If it’s not… I don’t want to hear it’s something like MS.

Thank you for telling me that. It makes complete sense to want it to be the simple answer. I won’t guess at a diagnosis today, but I also won’t tell you it’s tiredness when I don’t think that’s been shown. Is that fair?
SCA_MODELS.why: Validates the fear and is honest without catastrophising

SCA_MODELS.text: Yes. I’d rather know.

Here’s my thinking. Double vision that goes when either eye is covered points to the eye-moving nerves or muscles. The painful blurry episode sounds like inflammation of the nerve at the back of the eye, called optic neuritis. There are a few possible causes. One is MS. Another is a condition where muscles tire easily, called myasthenia, which fits it being worse in the evenings. None of these are confirmed, and the specialists need to examine you and do tests.
SCA_MODELS.why: Shares a reasoned differential in plain language

SCA_MODELS.text: So it could be MS?

It’s one of the things they’ll want to look for, and I’d rather you heard that from me honestly. MS is diagnosed by a neurologist, with a scan and an examination, and only if it meets strict criteria. Not everyone who has an episode like this goes on to have MS, and if it is MS, treatment is much better than it used to be.
SCA_MODELS.why: Answers directly, gives proportion without false reassurance

SCA_MODELS.text: Okay. That helps a bit.

What I can’t do over video is look properly at your eyes: your pupils, the eye movements, your eyelids when you look up for a while, and the back of your eyes. So I’d like you to come in today so a doctor can examine you face to face.
SCA_MODELS.why: Recognises video limits; arranges same-day in-person examination

SCA_MODELS.text: Today? Is that really necessary?

I think so. Depending on what we find, I’ll speak to the eye team or the neurologists today, and they’ll decide how quickly to see you and when to do a brain scan. I’ll also refer you to the neurologists about the eye episode and the double vision, marked urgent.
SCA_MODELS.why: Sets urgency by findings; same-day specialist advice; urgent neurology

SCA_MODELS.text: Okay. I can get there this afternoon.
One more practical thing. If you drive, please don’t while you’re getting double vision. The law says you must stop and tell the DVLA. When it’s controlled, driving can usually be looked at again.
SCA_MODELS.why: Gives the DVLA advice without inventing whether she drives

SCA_MODELS.text: Right. I hadn’t thought about that.

Before you come in, call 999 or go to A&E if you get a sudden severe headache, a painful eye with a drooping lid or one pupil much bigger, any trouble swallowing, slurred speech or breathing, or new weakness. Those would need attention straight away.
SCA_MODELS.why: Specific emergency safety-net in plain words

SCA_MODELS.text: Okay. Headache, pupil, swallowing, breathing, weakness.
Exactly that. So, can you tell me back what the plan is, so I know I’ve explained it properly?
Come in this afternoon to be examined, you’ll talk to the specialists, there’s an urgent referral, no driving with double vision, and 999 for those warning signs.
Perfect. I’ll ring you after the specialists have given their view so you’re not left waiting in the dark. Is there anything you’d like to ask?
SCA_MODELS.why: Defined follow-up and ownership of the result

SCA_MODELS.text: No. Thank you for being straight with me.

SCA_STEM.name: Erin Doyle
pmh: No significant past medical history recorded
No previous neurological or eye problems on the record
SCA_STEM.recent: No recent consultations. Booked an online video appointment herself.
SCA_STEM.reason: Video consultation: double vision on and off for a few weeks, and a recent few days of blurred, aching vision in the left eye.

SCA_KNOWLEDGE.guideline: [1] NICE NG220 (multiple sclerosis in adults, 2022, updated June 2026) · NICE NG12 Suspected cancer: recognition and referral (2015, last updated 15 April 2026) · [3] Association of British Neurologists myasthenia gravis management guidelines (2015, updated 2025) · [4] DVLA Assessing fitness to drive (visual disorders: diplopia) · [5] NICE NG228 (subarachnoid haemorrhage, 2022)
SCA_KNOWLEDGE.summary: Recurrent binocular double vision in a young woman, with a recent painful blurred-vision episode in one eye, is neurological until proved otherwise. Split monocular from binocular, screen for optic neuritis, fatigable weakness and red flags, get her examined in person today, and refer with the right urgency.

points.t: Ask whether the double image goes when either eye is covered. Monocular diplopia (persists through one eye alone) is usually ocular: refractive error, cataract, corneal or lens problems. Binocular diplopia (goes when either eye is covered) means the eyes are misaligned, from a cranial nerve, neuromuscular junction, muscle or orbital cause, and needs a neurological assessment.

A few days of blurred vision in one eye with pain, especially on eye movement, and duller colours is the classic story of optic neuritis. NICE NG220 [1]: if isolated optic neuritis is confirmed by an ophthalmologist, refer to a consultant neurologist; a consultant neurologist makes the diagnosis of MS using history, examination, MRI and the revised McDonald criteria (lesions disseminated in time and space). Diplopia from an internuclear ophthalmoplegia would be a second, separate site.

Fatigable weakness: double vision or drooping lids that worsen as the day goes on or with sustained gaze and improve with rest. Ask about chewing or swallowing fatigue, slurred or nasal speech, neck and limb weakness, and breathlessness. ABN guidelines [3]: diagnosis and treatment are specialist-led (AChR antibodies are positive in about half of purely ocular cases). Bulbar or breathing symptoms risk a myasthenic crisis and need emergency assessment.

A third nerve palsy with a dilated pupil, especially with headache or eye pain, is a posterior communicating artery aneurysm until proved otherwise: 999 or emergency department now. A sixth nerve palsy can be a false-localising sign of raised intracranial pressure: ask about headache worse lying down or on straining, vomiting and transient visual obscurations. Thunderclap headache peaking within minutes is a subarachnoid haemorrhage question (NICE NG228 [5]).

Acuity, colour vision, pupils including a relative afferent pupillary defect, eye movements in all directions with a cover test, ptosis and fatigability on sustained upgaze, fundi for disc swelling, and a brief neurological screen. None of this can be done reliably on video, so arrange an in-person examination today.

Emergency (999 or ED): pupil-involving third nerve palsy, thunderclap headache, bulbar or breathing symptoms, or signs of raised pressure with papilloedema. Same day: new persistent binocular diplopia or current visual loss, discussed with on-call ophthalmology or neurology. Urgent: suspected MS or ocular myasthenia once emergencies are excluded. NICE NG12 [2]: consider an urgent direct-access MRI brain (within 2 weeks) for progressive, sub-acute loss of central neurological function.

DVLA [4]: a driver with diplopia must stop driving and tell the DVLA. Driving may restart only once the DVLA accepts that the diplopia is controlled, for example with a patch or prisms. The patient holds the legal duty; the doctor advises and records the advice.

SCA_SC_TASKS.d: Open question; let her finish the story including the left-eye episode she mentioned almost in passing.
Work and screen use, how the symptoms affect her day, and whether she drives (asked neutrally, advice given conditionally).
Picked up “worse when tired”, the painful eye episode, and her hope that it’s “just eye strain”.
Her idea (eye strain), the unspoken fear (MS), and what she wanted (reassurance).
Same-day in-person examination: acuity, colour, pupils and RAPD, eye movements, fatigable ptosis, fundi, neuro screen.
Monocular versus binocular; optic neuritis and MS; ocular myasthenia; cranial nerve palsy; raised intracranial pressure.
Screened for pupil-involving third nerve palsy, thunderclap or raised-pressure headache, bulbar and breathing symptoms.
Binocular diplopia with probable optic neuritis: needs specialist neurological assessment, not tiredness.
Same-day examination and specialist advice; urgent neurology referral; MRI decided by specialists; honest explanation.
DVLA duty with diplopia; the impact on her work and anxiety.
Named 999 symptoms, a follow-up call after specialist advice, and teach-back.

social.t: Young adults with new neurological symptoms often explain them away (screens, stress, tiredness) because the alternative feels frightening. Naming the fear gently makes it possible to plan.
Double vision affects screen work, reading and travel. Temporary occlusion (a patch or frosted lens) may be advised by the specialist team; a fit note can cover time off work if needed.

legal.t: DVLA Assessing fitness to drive: a driver with diplopia must stop driving and notify the DVLA. Driving may resume only when the DVLA accepts the diplopia is controlled (for example patch or prisms). A later diagnosis such as MS or myasthenia has its own notification rules. The doctor advises and documents; the duty to notify is the patient’s.

professional.t: GMC remote consultations guidance: if a remote consultation cannot provide a safe assessment, arrange a face-to-face one. Eye movements, pupils and fundi need examination in person.
Share the possible causes honestly when asked, including MS, while being clear that nothing is confirmed. Document the discussion, the red-flag screen, the urgency set and the safety-net.

community.t: The MS Society and the Myaware charity provide information once a specialist diagnosis is made; do not signpost to condition-specific groups before diagnosis unless she asks.

redFlags: Painful third nerve palsy or a dilated pupil with ptosis: aneurysm until proved otherwise (999/ED)
Thunderclap headache, headache worse lying down or on straining, vomiting, transient visual obscurations (SAH or raised intracranial pressure)
Swallowing, speech or breathing difficulty with fatigable weakness (myasthenic crisis risk)
Persisting visual loss in one eye
psychosocial: Screen-based work and how the symptoms affect it
Her anxiety and tendency to explain symptoms away
ice: Idea: tiredness or eye strain from screens
Concern: unspoken fear of something serious such as MS
Expectation: to be reassured it is eye strain

SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosis: “Double vision that disappears when either eye is covered means the eyes aren’t lining up, so it comes from the nerves or muscles that move them. With the painful blurry episode in your left eye, which sounds like inflammation of the eye nerve, this needs a specialist neurological assessment rather than being put down to tiredness.”
SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosisLay: “Your two eyes are like a pair of cameras that have to point at exactly the same spot. When the double picture vanishes whichever eye you cover, it tells me the cameras are slightly out of line, and that’s about the wiring and the muscles, not tired eyes.”

management.reflectIce: “You said you’d been avoiding thinking about it because you were scared it might be MS. I’m not going to guess today, but I’m also not going to call it tiredness when I don’t think that’s been shown.”
management.psychosocial: Acknowledge the fear, give proportion (several possible causes; one episode does not always mean MS), and keep her involved in every step so she is not left waiting alone.
sharedPlan: Face-to-face examination today (acuity, colour, pupils/RAPD, eye movements, fatigable ptosis, fundi, neuro screen)
Same-day discussion with on-call ophthalmology or neurology based on findings
Urgent neurology referral; imaging and antibody tests per specialist advice
No driving while diplopic; notify the DVLA if she drives
safetyNet: 999/ED for sudden severe headache, painful eye with drooping lid or enlarged pupil, swallowing, speech or breathing difficulty, or new weakness
Call-back after the specialist view; review promptly if symptoms change

SCA_PITFALLS.intro: This station is failed by candidates who accept the patient’s own explanation. Binocular double vision plus a probable optic neuritis in a 29-year-old needs a proper neurological assessment, and the video format adds the trap of pretending to examine.

items.fail: Never asking whether the double vision goes when one eye is covered.
items.why: “Data gathering not sufficiently focused.” The monocular versus binocular split is the single most discriminating question in diplopia.
items.fix: Ask it in the first two minutes: “If you cover one eye, does it go? And the other eye?”

items.fail: Missing the painful blurred-vision episode because it was mentioned in passing.
items.why: Optic neuritis is the key clue to a demyelinating cause; missing it leads to a routine plan.
items.fix: Return to it: “Tell me more about the left eye. Did it hurt to move it? Were colours duller?”

items.fail: “Examining” pupils and eye movements over video and declaring them normal.
items.why: Unsafe and not credible. Examiners expect you to recognise the limits of a remote consultation.
items.fix: “I can’t check this properly on video. I’d like you examined in person today.”

items.fail: Reassuring her that it is eye strain because that is what she asked for.
items.why: “Colludes with the patient” and misses the hidden fear driving the minimisation.
items.fix: “I can hear you’d like it to be eye strain. I’ll be honest with you as we go.” Then ask whether she has wondered if it is more.

items.fail: Announcing “this could be MS” early, then listing its complications.
items.why: Catastrophising damages trust and is not supported until a neurologist has assessed her.
items.fix: Offer the differential honestly and proportionately: several possible causes, nothing confirmed, specialists will decide.

items.fail: Referring “urgently” with no timescale, no red-flag advice and no mention of driving.
items.why: Non-specific safety-netting and an omitted DVLA duty are standard failing feedback.
items.fix: Same-day examination, named 999 symptoms, conditional DVLA advice, and a promised call-back.
